paragraphs.text: After reading the short works that I recently composed for you, my dearest son Marcellinus, on the baptism of infants and on the perfection of human righteousness—namely that no one in this life seems either to have attained it or to be going to attain it, except for the one Mediator, who endured the human lot in the likeness of the flesh of sin, without any sin at all—you wrote back that you were troubled by my saying, in the second of the two books, that it is possible for a human being to be without sin, if his will is not lacking, with divine help assisting, and yet that, apart from the one in whom all will be given life, there had been or would be no one in whom this perfection existed while he lived here. For it seems absurd to you to say that something can happen for which an example is lacking, when, as I believe, you do not doubt that it has never happened that a camel passed through the eye of a needle, and yet he said that this too is possible for God. You may also read that twelve thousand legions of angels could have fought for Christ so that he would not suffer, but it did not happen. You may read that it could have happened that the nations were driven out all at once from the land that was being given to the children of Israel, but that God nevertheless willed it to happen gradually. And six hundred other things can come to mind that we admit either could have happened or can happen, and yet we cannot produce examples of their having happened. Therefore we ought not to deny that it is possible for a human being to be without sin simply because there is no human being in whom we can demonstrate this to have been brought to perfection, apart from the one who is not only man but also God by nature.

flags.note: perfectio is rendered ‘perfection’ (no glossary row; the term recurs through the treatise). In the last sentence id esse perfectum is rendered ‘this ... brought to perfection’ to keep the echo of perfectio; id is the state of being without sin.

flags.quoteTarget: in the likeness of the flesh of sin
flags.note: Quotation of Rom. 8:3 woven into the sentence, translated as the author’s text from his Latin (the Vulgate has in similitudinem carnis peccati). The genitive is kept literally, ‘the flesh of sin’, and not smoothed to ‘sinful flesh’; the reviewer may prefer the latter.

flags.quoteTarget: in whom all will be given life
flags.note: Quotation of 1 Cor. 15:22 (in Christo omnes vivificabuntur) with the relative pronoun in place of the name. vivificare is ‘give life’, as in the profile.

flags.quoteSource: ille hoc quoque dixit Deo esse possibile
flags.quoteTarget: he said that this too is possible for God
flags.note: ille is the Lord (the saying on the camel and the needle, Matt. 19:24–26 and parallels), not named in the Latin. Rendered ‘he’ in lower case so as not to add ‘the Lord’; the reviewer may prefer ‘the Lord’ for clarity.

Paraphrase of Matt. 26:53, where the Vulgate has ‘more than twelve legions of angels’; the Latin of the edition has twelve thousand legions. Translated as written, not corrected. To verify against the critical apparatus whether this is Augustine’s own reading or a variant.

flags.quoteTarget: driven out all at once from the land
flags.note: exterminare: ‘drive out’ (the classical sense; Exod. 23:29–30 speaks of driving the nations out little by little) or ‘destroy’ (Deut. 7:22 speaks of consuming them little by little). ‘Exterminated’ is avoided as a false friend. The allusion is identified by the translator; the Latin names no passage.
sexcenta is the Latin idiom for ‘a great many’. The number is kept as written (numbers in words stay words); it reads as a hyperbole in English as well.

notes: Chapter I, one paragraph (De spiritu et littera 1.1). The job carries no references; the biblical material was identified by the translator and is listed in scripture (Rom. 8:3 and 1 Cor. 15:22 are woven-in quotations, the rest allusions; the Old Testament parallels for the gradual expulsion of the nations are to be confirmed). Choices to review: carnis peccati kept as ‘the flesh of sin’; ‘twelve thousand legions’ translated as written; exterminarentur as ‘driven out’; ille as ‘he’; sexcenta kept as ‘six hundred’; humana perpessus est as ‘endured the human lot’. The long first sentence keeps the structure of the Latin (ablative absolute, then the main verb rescripsisti); the colons of the edition are rendered with full stops, and the second sentence is divided at the colons without loss.
